questions.question: What is a functional interface in Java?
questions.title: Functional Interface in Java 8
questions.direct_answer: A functional interface has exactly one abstract method (SAM — Single Abstract Method). It can have multiple default and static methods. The @FunctionalInterface annotation verifies this at compile time. Functional interfaces are the target type for lambda expressions.

interviewer_intent.testing: Foundational Java 8 knowledge — functional interfaces are the contract for lambdas
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking @FunctionalInterface creates the constraint — the annotation only validates it
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name the four key built-in functional interfaces: Predicate, Function, Consumer, Supplier

sections.title: The Foundation of Lambda Expressions
sections.content: A **functional interface** is the bridge between traditional Java interfaces and modern lambda expressions. It's an interface with exactly **one abstract method** (called the SAM — Single Abstract Method). Think of it like a contract: "I promise to do one thing, and one thing only." This single method becomes the target for lambda expressions. The **@FunctionalInterface** annotation is optional but recommended — it tells the compiler to verify the rule, preventing you from accidentally adding a second abstract method later. A functional interface can have multiple **default methods** and **static methods** because these have implementations and don't count toward the "one abstract method" rule. Built-in examples include **Runnable** (run method), **Callable<V>** (call method), and the Java 8 additions like **Predicate<T>**, **Function<T,R>**, **Consumer<T>**, and **Supplier<T>**. Without functional interfaces, we couldn't write `list.forEach(item -> System.out.println(item))` — the lambda needs a target type.

sections.title: Custom Functional Interface for Order Validation
Key Points
content: **SAM (Single Abstract Method)**: exactly one abstract method defines the contract for the lambda expression
**@FunctionalInterface**: optional annotation that enforces the single abstract method rule at compile time
**Default methods**: functional interfaces can have multiple default methods with implementations without breaking the SAM rule
**Static methods**: allowed in functional interfaces and don't count toward the abstract method count
**Lambda target type**: the compiler matches lambda signatures to the functional interface's abstract method
**Built-in examples**: Runnable, Callable, Comparator were functional interfaces before Java 8 even existed
**Java 8 additions**: Predicate, Function, Consumer, Supplier are the four fundamental functional interfaces in java.util.function

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A functional interface is an interface with exactly one abstract method. It's the foundation that makes lambda expressions work in Java. The at-FunctionalInterface annotation is optional but recommended because it tells the compiler to verify you've got only one abstract method. If you accidentally add a second one later, the compiler will catch it. The interface can still have multiple default methods and static methods because those have implementations and don't count. Think of Runnable as the classic example — it's got just the run method, and you can write a lambda for it. Java 8 introduced four key functional interfaces in the java.util.function package: Predicate for testing conditions, Function for transforming data, Consumer for performing actions, and Supplier for producing values. The common mistake freshers make is thinking you must use the annotation for an interface to work with lambdas. You don't — any interface with one abstract method works. The annotation just adds compile-time safety. When I create custom functional interfaces, I always use the annotation to prevent future mistakes when the codebase evolves.

questions.question: What is the difference between Predicate, Function, Consumer, and Supplier?
questions.title: Predicate vs Function vs Consumer vs Supplier
questions.direct_answer: Predicate<T>: T → boolean (test/filter). Function<T,R>: T → R (transform). Consumer<T>: T → void (side effect). Supplier<T>: () → T (produce). These four cover the four fundamental patterns of what a function can do.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can name and distinguish the four key functional interfaces
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing Function and Consumer — Function returns something, Consumer does not
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a concrete real-world use case for each from Stream operations

sections.title: The Four Pillars of Functional Programming in Java
sections.content: These four interfaces represent the fundamental operations you can perform with functions. **Predicate<T>** answers yes/no questions — it takes an input and returns a boolean. **Function<T,R>** transforms data — it takes input type T and produces output type R. **Consumer<T>** performs side effects — it takes an input but returns nothing (void). **Supplier<T>** produces values — it takes no input but returns type T. Together, they cover every basic lambda pattern: testing, transforming, acting, and creating. Understanding when to use each is critical for readable Stream operations and functional composition.

sections.title: Choosing the Right Interface
sections.content: Use **Predicate** when you're making decisions or filtering collections — like finding all active users or orders above a certain amount. The boolean return tells you whether something passes the test. Use **Function** when you're transforming data — converting a User to a DTO, extracting a field, or parsing a string to an integer. Use **Consumer** when you're performing actions without returning values — logging, sending emails, updating databases, or printing to console. The void return signals it's about side effects. Use **Supplier** when you're creating or providing values lazily — generating random numbers, lazy initialization, or factory patterns. The lack of input parameters means it's purely about production.

sections.title: Real-World Usage in Order Processing
Key Points
content: **Predicate<T>**: boolean test(T t) — used in filter operations, returns true/false for decision making
**Function<T,R>**: R apply(T t) — used in map operations, transforms input type T to output type R
**Consumer<T>**: void accept(T t) — used in forEach operations, performs action with no return value
**Supplier<T>**: T get() — used in generate operations, produces values without taking input
**Composition methods**: Predicate has and/or/negate, Function has andThen/compose, Consumer has andThen
**BiFunction variants**: BiPredicate, BiFunction, BiConsumer exist for two-parameter operations
**Return type is key**: Function returns something, Consumer returns nothing — this is the critical difference

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: These are the four fundamental functional interfaces in Java's java.util.function package. Predicate takes an input and returns a boolean — it's for testing conditions. You use it in stream filter operations. Function takes an input and returns a different output — it transforms data. You use it in map operations. Consumer takes an input but returns nothing — it's for side effects like logging or saving to a database. You use it in forEach. Supplier takes no input but returns a value — it produces or generates data. You use it with Stream.generate or for lazy initialization. The key difference people confuse is Function versus Consumer. Function returns something, Consumer doesn't. If you need the result, use Function. If you're just doing something like printing or updating, use Consumer. In real code, you'd use Predicate to filter orders above a thousand dollars, Function to convert orders to DTOs, Consumer to send email notifications, and Supplier to generate unique IDs. Each one maps to a specific Stream operation, which makes streams so powerful and readable.

questions.question: What is @FunctionalInterface annotation and is it required?
questions.title: @FunctionalInterface Annotation in Java
questions.direct_answer: @FunctionalInterface is an optional annotation that tells the compiler to verify the interface has exactly one abstract method. It is NOT required — any interface with one abstract method can be used as a functional interface. The annotation just prevents accidental addition of a second abstract method.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding that @FunctionalInterface is optional but recommended
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking an interface MUST have @FunctionalInterface to be used as a lambda target
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that Runnable and Callable work as functional interfaces without @FunctionalInterface on them

sections.title: Compile-Time Safety for Functional Interfaces
sections.content: The **@FunctionalInterface** annotation is a compile-time safety mechanism, not a runtime requirement. It's like a seatbelt — you don't need it to drive, but it protects you from mistakes. Any interface with exactly one abstract method is automatically a functional interface, whether or not it has this annotation. **Runnable** and **Callable** are functional interfaces and have been since Java 1.0 and 1.5 respectively, long before the annotation existed. The annotation does two things: it documents your intent ("I designed this to be used with lambdas") and it enforces the single abstract method rule at compile time. If you annotate an interface with **@FunctionalInterface** and then add a second abstract method, the compiler throws an error immediately. Without the annotation, you wouldn't know until you tried to use a lambda and got a confusing error. The annotation prevents future developers from breaking your interface by accident during refactoring.

sections.title: Functional Interface With and Without Annotation
Key Points
content: **Optional annotation**: @FunctionalInterface is not required for an interface to be used with lambdas
**Compile-time verification**: the annotation makes the compiler enforce the single abstract method rule
**Documentation value**: signals to developers that the interface is designed for lambda usage
**Prevents breaking changes**: stops accidental addition of second abstract method during refactoring
**Historic interfaces**: Runnable, Callable, Comparator work as functional interfaces without the annotation
**Default methods allowed**: interfaces with @FunctionalInterface can have multiple default and static methods
**Best practice**: always use @FunctionalInterface when designing an interface for lambda usage

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The at-FunctionalInterface annotation is optional. You don't need it for an interface to work with lambdas. Any interface with exactly one abstract method is automatically a functional interface. Runnable is the perfect example — it's been a functional interface since Java 1.0, way before the annotation existed in Java 8. So what does the annotation do? It tells the compiler to verify the rule. If you put at-FunctionalInterface on an interface and then accidentally add a second abstract method, you get a compile error immediately. Without the annotation, the interface just stops being a functional interface silently, and you only find out when your lambda doesn't compile. The annotation also documents your intent. When another developer sees it, they know you designed this interface specifically for lambda usage. It's a safety net during refactoring. The common mistake is thinking you must add the annotation for lambdas to work. You don't. But you should use it anyway because it prevents future bugs. I always annotate my functional interfaces even though it's optional, just like I always use Override even though that's optional too.

questions.question: How do you compose two Predicates in Java 8?
questions.title: Composing Predicates in Java 8
questions.direct_answer: Predicate has default methods and(), or(), and negate() for composition. p1.and(p2) creates a new Predicate that is true only when both are true. p1.or(p2) is true when either is true. p.negate() inverts the Predicate.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical Java 8 Predicate composition — shows real usage beyond just definitions
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using && inside a lambda instead of and() method — works but misses the composition approach
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show how composed predicates make stream filters more readable and reusable

sections.title: Building Complex Logic from Simple Predicates
sections.content: **Predicate composition** is one of Java 8's most elegant features — it lets you build complex filtering logic from simple, reusable pieces. The **Predicate** interface provides three default methods for composition: **and()**, **or()**, and **negate()**. Think of them like building blocks: `isActive.and(isPremium)` creates a new Predicate that's only true when both conditions are true. `isStudent.or(isSenior)` is true when either condition is true. `isExpired.negate()` inverts the logic — true becomes false, false becomes true. This is more powerful than using logical operators (&&, ||, !) inside a single lambda because each predicate is named, testable, and reusable. You can define `isHighValue` once and compose it with different predicates throughout your codebase. The composed predicates are themselves Predicates, so you can pass them to **Stream.filter()** or compose them further. This creates self-documenting, modular filtering logic.

sections.title: Composing Order Filters for Complex Business Rules
Key Points
content: **and() method**: combines two predicates with logical AND — both must be true for the result to be true
**or() method**: combines two predicates with logical OR — either can be true for the result to be true
**negate() method**: inverts a predicate — true becomes false, false becomes true
**Reusability**: composed predicates can be stored in variables and reused across multiple streams
**Readability**: isHighValue.and(isPending) reads better than combining conditions inside a lambda
**Short-circuit evaluation**: and() stops evaluating if first predicate is false, or() stops if first is true
**Chain composition**: you can chain multiple compositions like p1.and(p2).or(p3).negate()

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Predicate composition lets you build complex filtering logic from simple, reusable predicates. The Predicate interface gives you three methods: and, or, and negate. If you've got isHighValue and isPending predicates, you can write isHighValue.and(isPending) to create a new predicate that's only true when both are true. The or method works similarly — isStudent.or(isSenior) is true when either condition passes. The negate method flips the logic — if isExpired is true, isExpired.negate() is false. The key advantage over using double-ampersand or double-pipe operators inside a lambda is reusability and readability. Each predicate has a name that explains what it does. You can test each one independently. You can compose them in different ways throughout your code. In stream operations, this makes filters incredibly readable. Instead of a messy lambda with multiple conditions, you write filter(isHighValue.and(isPending).or(isPriority)), and anyone reading the code immediately understands the business logic. The composed result is itself a Predicate, so you can keep composing or pass it to any method expecting a Predicate. It's functional programming at its best — small, focused functions combined into complex behavior.

questions.question: What is Function.andThen() vs Function.compose() in Java?
questions.title: Function.andThen() vs Function.compose()
questions.direct_answer: f.andThen(g) means: apply f first, then apply g to the result (f → g). f.compose(g) means: apply g first, then apply f to the result (g → f). andThen is more intuitive for left-to-right reading.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of Function composition methods — shows depth of Java 8 knowledge
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Getting the order backwards for compose()
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show with types: f: A→B, g: B→C, f.andThen(g) gives A→C

sections.title: Two Ways to Chain Function Transformations
sections.content: **Function composition** lets you build data transformation pipelines by chaining functions together. The **Function** interface provides two composition methods that do the same thing in opposite orders. **andThen(g)** means "do this function first, then do g" — it's left-to-right execution matching how we read code. **compose(g)** means "do g first, then do this function" — it's right-to-left execution like mathematical function composition. If `f` transforms type A to B, and `g` transforms B to C, then `f.andThen(g)` gives you a function from A to C. The same result happens with `g.compose(f)`. Most developers find `andThen` more intuitive because it matches the execution order you'd write in procedural code. Both create a new Function — the original functions are unchanged.

sections.title: Choosing Between andThen and compose
sections.content: Use **andThen()** when you're building transformation pipelines that match your mental model of "do this, then do that." If you're converting a User to a DTO, then converting the DTO to JSON, write `toDTO.andThen(toJson)` — it reads naturally. This is the preferred choice for most business logic because it matches procedural thinking. Use **compose()** when you're working with mathematical function composition or when you need to pre-process input before your main function runs. If you have a main function `processOrder` and need to validate the input first, `processOrder.compose(validateOrder)` expresses "compose this by adding validation first." In practice, andThen is used 90% of the time because it's more intuitive. You'll rarely see compose in production code unless the team has a strong functional programming background.

sections.title: Price Calculation Pipeline with Function Composition
Key Points
content: **andThen(g)**: executes current function first, then g — left-to-right execution order
**compose(g)**: executes g first, then current function — right-to-left execution order
**Type safety**: f.andThen(g) requires output type of f to match input type of g
**Creates new Function**: both methods return a new Function without modifying the originals
**Equivalent results**: f.andThen(g) produces the same result as g.compose(f) for the same inputs
**Readability preference**: andThen is more commonly used because it matches procedural code flow
**Chain multiple times**: you can chain multiple andThen or compose calls to build complex pipelines

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: These are two methods on the Function interface that let you chain transformations together. andThen means do this function first, then do the next one. compose means do the other function first, then do this one. So if you've got a function f that converts A to B, and a function g that converts B to C, then f.andThen(g) gives you a function that goes from A to C. It applies f first, takes the result, and feeds it to g. With compose it's backwards — f.compose(g) applies g first, then f. Most people find andThen more intuitive because it reads left to right like normal code. If you're building a pricing pipeline, you'd write extractPrice.andThen(applyDiscount).andThen(applyTax), and it reads exactly how it executes. The common mistake is mixing up the order with compose. Remember: f.compose(g) applies g first, even though g appears after compose in the code. In real projects, you'll see andThen way more often than compose because it matches how we naturally think about sequential steps. Both create a new Function object — they don't modify the originals. You can keep chaining them to build complex transformation pipelines.

questions.question: How do you create a custom functional interface in Java?
questions.title: Custom Functional Interface in Java
questions.direct_answer: Define an interface with exactly one abstract method and annotate it with @FunctionalInterface. Choose the method signature to match what your lambda will do. Custom functional interfaces are needed when none of the built-in ones (Predicate, Function, etc.) match your signature.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to create reusable functional interfaces for domain-specific operations
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Creating a custom functional interface when Function<T,R> or BiFunction would already work
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a practical example: a functional interface that throws checked exceptions

sections.title: Designing Domain-Specific Functional Contracts
sections.content: Creating a custom functional interface is straightforward: define an interface with **exactly one abstract method**, choose a method signature that matches your domain logic, and annotate it with **@FunctionalInterface** for compile-time safety. You need a custom interface when the built-in ones (Predicate, Function, Consumer, Supplier) don't match your requirements. Common scenarios include: (1) **methods that throw checked exceptions** (built-in interfaces don't throw), (2) **domain-specific operations** with meaningful names like `OrderProcessor.processOrder(Order order)` instead of generic `Function.apply`, (3) **multiple parameters** with specific types where BiFunction<T,U,R> feels too generic, and (4) **operations combining multiple built-in patterns** like taking two inputs and returning void. The interface name and method name should clearly communicate intent. A custom **PaymentProcessor** with a **processPayment** method is more readable than `Function<PaymentRequest, PaymentResult>`. Default methods can add composition logic just like Predicate.and() or Function.andThen().

sections.title: Custom Functional Interface for Exception-Throwing Operations
Key Points
content: **Single abstract method**: the interface must have exactly one abstract method to be functional
**@FunctionalInterface annotation**: always add this to get compile-time verification of the SAM rule
**Checked exceptions**: custom interfaces can declare checked exceptions, built-in ones cannot
**Domain names**: use meaningful names like OrderValidator instead of generic Function<Order, Boolean>
**Default methods**: add composition helpers like and, or, andThen to make your interface more powerful
**When to create**: only when built-in interfaces (Predicate, Function, Consumer, Supplier, BiFunction) don't fit
**Avoid over-engineering**: if Function<T,R> works, don't create a custom interface just for a different name

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Creating a custom functional interface is simple. You define an interface with exactly one abstract method and annotate it with at-FunctionalInterface. The method signature should match what your lambda will do — the parameter types it takes and the return type it produces. The most common reason to create a custom one is when you need to throw checked exceptions. The built-in interfaces like Function and Consumer don't throw checked exceptions, so if you're doing file I/O or database operations, you need a custom interface. Another reason is domain clarity. If you're processing orders, an OrderProcessor interface with a processOrder method is way more readable than Function<Order, Result>. It tells the next developer exactly what the lambda is supposed to do. You can also add default methods for composition, just like Predicate has and and or. The mistake freshers make is creating custom interfaces when Function or BiFunction would work fine. If you're just transforming one type to another and don't need exception handling, use Function. Only create custom interfaces when you've got a specific requirement the built-ins don't cover. When I create one, I always add the at-FunctionalInterface annotation for safety, give it a domain-specific name, and document what the method should do.

sections.title: Performance-Optimized Functional Interfaces for Primitives
sections.content: Java provides **primitive-specialized functional interfaces** to avoid the performance cost of **autoboxing** — the automatic conversion between primitives (int, long, double) and their wrapper objects (Integer, Long, Double). When you use `Function<Integer, Integer>` with an IntStream, every int gets boxed into an Integer object, processed, and unboxed back to int. This creates millions of temporary objects in high-throughput scenarios. The primitive interfaces like **IntPredicate**, **IntFunction<R>**, **ToIntFunction<T>**, **IntConsumer**, **IntUnaryOperator**, and their long/double equivalents work directly with primitive values. **IntStream**, **LongStream**, and **DoubleStream** use these interfaces automatically — when you call `intStream.filter(predicate)`, it expects an **IntPredicate**, not a `Predicate<Integer>`. The naming pattern is consistent: **IntPredicate** tests an int, **ToIntFunction<T>** converts T to int, **IntFunction<R>** converts int to R, **IntUnaryOperator** transforms int to int. Using these specialized interfaces can improve performance by 2-10x in tight loops processing millions of values.

sections.title: Primitive Interfaces vs Generic Interfaces in Streams
Key Points
content: **Autoboxing cost**: converting int to Integer creates an object — expensive in loops processing millions of values
**IntPredicate/LongPredicate/DoublePredicate**: test primitives without boxing, used in filter operations
**IntUnaryOperator/LongUnaryOperator/DoubleUnaryOperator**: transform primitive to same type (int → int)
**ToIntFunction/ToLongFunction/ToDoubleFunction**: convert any object to a primitive for mapToInt/mapToLong/mapToDouble
**IntFunction/LongFunction/DoubleFunction**: convert primitive to an object type
**IntConsumer/LongConsumer/DoubleConsumer**: consume primitives in forEach without boxing
**Primitive streams**: IntStream, LongStream, DoubleStream use these specialized interfaces automatically

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Primitive functional interfaces are specialized versions that work directly with int, long, and double values to avoid autoboxing overhead. Autoboxing is when Java automatically converts a primitive like int into an Integer object. That's fine for small operations, but if you're processing a million numbers in a stream, you're creating a million temporary Integer objects. That kills performance. Java provides interfaces like IntPredicate, IntFunction, IntConsumer, and IntUnaryOperator that work with raw int values. When you use an IntStream and call filter, it expects an IntPredicate, not a Predicate<Integer>. The naming pattern is consistent. IntPredicate tests an int, ToIntFunction converts something to an int, IntFunction converts an int to something else, and IntUnaryOperator transforms int to int. The same pattern exists for long and double. If you're working with primitive streams — IntStream, LongStream, DoubleStream — you automatically use these specialized interfaces. The performance difference matters in real applications. I've seen stream operations run five times faster just by switching from Stream<Integer> to IntStream with primitive interfaces. The common mistake is using Function<Integer, Integer> when IntUnaryOperator would avoid all the boxing. Always use the primitive versions when you're working with numeric streams.

speakable_v2.hook: When you use Function of Integer to Integer with a million numbers, you're boxing every single int into an object. Primitive functional interfaces eliminate that entirely.

beats.text: Every time you use Function of Integer to Integer, each primitive int gets wrapped in an Integer object. That's object allocation and garbage collection pressure for every element in your pipeline. With a small list it doesn't matter. With millions of numbers it adds up.

Java provides primitive-specialized versions of all the main functional interfaces. IntPredicate is int to boolean — no boxing. IntUnaryOperator is int to int — no boxing. ToIntFunction takes a T and returns a plain int. The whole family exists for int, long, and double.

When you use IntStream instead of Stream of Integer, all the operations automatically use these primitive interfaces internally. So just choosing IntStream over Stream gets you the performance benefit without having to think about which primitive interface to pick.

non-obvious: for a typical web application processing a list of 50 users, the boxing overhead is invisible. Primitive interfaces matter for batch processing, numerical algorithms, or any pipeline with millions of elements. Don't prematurely optimize — profile first.
